subtopics.title: word analogy
subtopics.teaching: Word analogies compare the relationship between two words and apply the same relationship to another pair.
subtopics.worked_example: 'Book : read :: food : eat' follows object-to-associated action.
subtopics.pitfall: Sharing a topic is not enough if the relationship differs.
subtopics.mastery: Identify the exact relation before selecting the answer.

subtopics.title: number analogy
subtopics.teaching: Number analogies use a mathematical relationship between one pair and apply it to another pair.
subtopics.worked_example: If 3 : 9 follows ×3, then 5 : 15 follows the same rule.
subtopics.pitfall: A rule that fits one pair but not the complete question is insufficient.
subtopics.mastery: Test the same operation consistently on all given pairs.

subtopics.title: figure analogy
subtopics.teaching: Figure analogies compare transformations such as rotation, reflection, movement, addition or removal of elements.
subtopics.worked_example: If a dot moves clockwise by one position in the first transformation, apply the same movement to the second figure.
subtopics.pitfall: A visual answer may look similar without preserving the transformation.
subtopics.mastery: Track each changed feature systematically.

subtopics.title: classification
subtopics.teaching: Classification groups items according to a common property such as category, function, structure or numerical rule.
subtopics.worked_example: Triangle, square and circle can be grouped as geometric figures, while a number differs under that rule.
subtopics.pitfall: An item can fit multiple categories, so the intended rule must explain the full group.
subtopics.mastery: State and apply one consistent classification rule.

subtopics.title: odd one out
subtopics.teaching: Odd-one-out problems identify the item that breaks the relationship shared by the others.
subtopics.worked_example: 2, 4, 6 and 9 differ because the first three are even while 9 is odd.
subtopics.pitfall: An alternative property may exist, so use the simplest rule supported by the set.
subtopics.mastery: Identify the majority rule before selecting the exception.

subtopics.title: number series
subtopics.teaching: Number series require finding the rule connecting consecutive terms, often using differences, ratios or alternating operations.
subtopics.worked_example: 2, 5, 8, 11 increases by 3 each time, so the next term is 14.
subtopics.pitfall: Checking only the first two differences can miss an alternating pattern.
subtopics.mastery: Test the proposed rule across every transition.

subtopics.title: alphabet series
subtopics.teaching: Alphabet series apply ordered letter positions, skips, reversals or repeated patterns.
subtopics.worked_example: A, C, E, G advances by two alphabet positions, giving I next.
subtopics.pitfall: Treating letters only as visual symbols can hide their positional pattern.
subtopics.mastery: Convert letters to positions when useful and verify the step pattern.

subtopics.title: mixed series
subtopics.teaching: Mixed series combine numbers, letters or symbols and may use separate interleaved rules.
subtopics.worked_example: A1, C3, E5 follows two linked progressions: letters advance by two and numbers increase by two.
subtopics.pitfall: A single-rule assumption may fail when two patterns alternate.
subtopics.mastery: Separate components and test each pattern independently.

subtopics.title: figure series
subtopics.teaching: Figure series use repeated visual changes such as rotation, movement, count, shading or shape transformation.
subtopics.worked_example: If a triangle rotates 90 degrees clockwise at each step, the next figure continues the same rotation.
subtopics.pitfall: Focusing on shape alone can miss movement or shading changes.
subtopics.mastery: Track every changing attribute across the sequence.

subtopics.title: missing terms
subtopics.teaching: A missing-term problem asks for the value or figure that preserves the established sequence rule.
subtopics.worked_example: In 4, 8, 16, ?, 64, each term doubles, so the missing value is 32.
subtopics.pitfall: Choosing a number that fits only one neighbour is not enough.
subtopics.mastery: Check the missing term against both preceding and following relationships.

subtopics.title: letter coding
subtopics.teaching: Letter coding maps letters to other letters using a defined transformation such as shifting alphabet positions.
subtopics.worked_example: If CAT becomes DBU by shifting every letter forward one place, DOG becomes EPH under the same rule.
subtopics.pitfall: A transformation should be applied consistently to every relevant character.
subtopics.mastery: Identify the letter-position rule and apply it uniformly.

subtopics.title: number coding
subtopics.teaching: Number coding represents words or letters using numerical values based on a stated or discoverable rule.
subtopics.worked_example: If A=1, B=2 and C=3, then CAB can be represented as 3-1-2.
subtopics.pitfall: Different questions may use different coding schemes, so do not assume one universal code.
subtopics.mastery: Infer the coding rule from the examples before decoding.

subtopics.title: symbol coding
subtopics.teaching: Symbol coding replaces letters, numbers or categories with symbols according to an established mapping.
subtopics.worked_example: If ▲ represents A and ● represents B, the coded form of AB is ▲●.
subtopics.pitfall: A symbol has no assumed meaning outside the rule given by the question.
subtopics.mastery: Build the mapping table and decode only after all relevant assignments are clear.

subtopics.title: transformations
subtopics.teaching: Coding transformations may reverse order, shift positions, substitute values or combine multiple operations.
subtopics.worked_example: If a word is reversed and then each letter is shifted one position, both operations must be applied in that order.
subtopics.pitfall: Applying the right operations in the wrong order can produce a different code.
subtopics.mastery: Write each transformation as a separate step and preserve the sequence.

subtopics.title: coded relationships
subtopics.teaching: Some coding questions encode relationships between words or objects rather than individual letters.
subtopics.worked_example: If one code indicates 'A is the parent of B,' decoding requires identifying the relationship represented rather than translating letters.
subtopics.pitfall: A familiar-looking code should not be interpreted without its examples.
subtopics.mastery: Use the given coded examples to reconstruct the relationship rule.

subtopics.title: family relations
subtopics.teaching: Family-relation problems represent kinship links such as parent, sibling, child, uncle, aunt and cousin.
subtopics.worked_example: If Ravi is Maya's brother and Maya is Arun's mother, Ravi is Arun's maternal uncle.
subtopics.pitfall: Gender and generation must both be tracked.
subtopics.mastery: Translate each relationship into a simple family tree before answering.

subtopics.title: blood relations
subtopics.teaching: Blood-relation questions require combining multiple kinship statements while distinguishing direct and indirect relationships.
subtopics.worked_example: If A is B's mother and B is C's brother, A is C's mother if B and C share that parent as stated or implied by the problem.
subtopics.pitfall: Do not add unstated relationships merely because they are common in real life.
subtopics.mastery: Use only relationships supported by the question.

subtopics.title: directions
subtopics.teaching: Direction problems use compass relationships such as north, south, east and west and may include turns.
subtopics.worked_example: If a person walks north and then turns right, the new direction is east.
subtopics.pitfall: Left and right depend on the person's current facing direction.
subtopics.mastery: Track orientation after every movement or turn.

subtopics.title: distance
subtopics.teaching: Distance problems combine movements to determine displacement or total path length depending on the question.
subtopics.worked_example: Walking 3 km east and 4 km north gives a 5 km straight-line displacement using the 3-4-5 triangle, while the path travelled is 7 km.
subtopics.pitfall: Distance travelled and displacement are not always the same quantity.
subtopics.mastery: Determine which distance concept the question asks for before calculating.

subtopics.title: position problems
subtopics.teaching: Position problems determine relative location using rows, columns, directions or movement constraints.
subtopics.worked_example: If A is third from the left and B is immediately to A's right, B is fourth from the left.
subtopics.pitfall: A position stated from the right must be converted carefully when total positions are known.
subtopics.mastery: Represent positions on a line or grid and apply each constraint in order.

subtopics.title: rank problems
subtopics.teaching: Rank problems determine an item's position from the top, bottom, left or right using stated relationships.
subtopics.worked_example: If a student is 7th from the top and there are 20 students, the same student is 14th from the bottom.
subtopics.pitfall: Use total count plus one when converting opposite ranks.
subtopics.mastery: Convert ranks carefully and check the total-position relationship.

subtopics.title: comparison chains
subtopics.teaching: Comparison chains combine statements such as taller than, older than or faster than to establish an order.
subtopics.worked_example: If A>B and B>C, then A>C by transitivity for the stated comparison.
subtopics.pitfall: A chain cannot reverse direction without evidence.
subtopics.mastery: Build the chain explicitly before selecting a relative position.

subtopics.title: arrangements
subtopics.teaching: Arrangement problems place people or objects in positions subject to constraints such as adjacency, fixed positions or exclusions.
subtopics.worked_example: If A must sit beside B and C must be at an end, place the fixed constraint first and test remaining positions.
subtopics.pitfall: Starting with unconstrained items can create unnecessary cases.
subtopics.mastery: Place the strongest constraints first and verify every condition.

subtopics.title: scheduling
subtopics.teaching: Scheduling problems assign activities to time slots while respecting order, availability or separation rules.
subtopics.worked_example: If a meeting must occur before lunch and another event must follow it, place the dependency before filling free slots.
subtopics.pitfall: A schedule that fits one condition but violates another is invalid.
subtopics.mastery: Represent time slots explicitly and test every scheduling constraint.

subtopics.title: ordering constraints
subtopics.teaching: Ordering constraints specify relative positions such as before, after, immediately before or between.
subtopics.worked_example: If A is before B and C is immediately after B, the sequence A-B-C must preserve both relationships.
subtopics.pitfall: 'Before' does not mean immediately before unless stated.
subtopics.mastery: Distinguish strict order from adjacency and apply each constraint exactly.

subtopics.title: statements and conclusions
subtopics.teaching: Statement-and-conclusion questions ask whether a conclusion necessarily follows from the information given.
subtopics.worked_example: If all registered students have IDs and Ravi is a registered student, Ravi has an ID follows directly.
subtopics.pitfall: A conclusion that is merely possible is weaker than one logically guaranteed.
subtopics.mastery: Use only the stated premises and test whether the conclusion must be true.

subtopics.title: syllogisms
subtopics.teaching: Syllogisms use categorical statements to determine what logically follows from relationships between groups.
subtopics.worked_example: If all A are B and all B are C, then all A are C.
subtopics.pitfall: The reverse conclusion that all C are A does not follow.
subtopics.mastery: Represent group relationships and avoid reversing one-way statements.

subtopics.title: cause and effect
subtopics.teaching: Cause-and-effect reasoning identifies whether one event plausibly produces another and distinguishes it from simple sequence or association.
subtopics.worked_example: If a machine stops because its power supply fails, the power failure is a stated cause of the shutdown.
subtopics.pitfall: Two events occurring together do not automatically prove causation.
subtopics.mastery: Look for explicit mechanisms or evidence before claiming cause and effect.

subtopics.title: assumptions
subtopics.teaching: An assumption is an unstated idea that must be accepted for a statement or argument to work.
subtopics.worked_example: A school proposes online registration because it assumes students can access the registration system.
subtopics.pitfall: An assumption is not simply another fact mentioned in the argument.
subtopics.mastery: Identify the missing condition on which the argument depends.

subtopics.title: decision logic
subtopics.teaching: Decision logic applies explicit rules and constraints to choose among alternatives.
subtopics.worked_example: If a trip requires a valid ID AND parental permission, missing either requirement prevents eligibility.
subtopics.pitfall: Replacing AND with OR changes the decision rule.
subtopics.mastery: Translate every condition into a logical test before deciding.

subtopics.title: seating arrangements
subtopics.teaching: Seating puzzles require placing people around rows or circles while respecting adjacency, opposition and positional constraints.
subtopics.worked_example: In a row, if A sits immediately left of B, the pair can be treated as a block before considering other placements.
subtopics.pitfall: Circular arrangements require attention to relative positions rather than an arbitrary first seat.
subtopics.mastery: Draw the arrangement and apply fixed or strongest constraints first.

subtopics.title: distribution
subtopics.teaching: Distribution puzzles allocate objects, people or quantities across groups subject to totals, limits or uniqueness rules.
subtopics.worked_example: If 12 books are distributed equally among 3 shelves, each shelf receives 4 books.
subtopics.pitfall: A distribution can satisfy the total while violating a per-group limit.
subtopics.mastery: Track totals and every stated minimum, maximum or equality constraint.

subtopics.title: matching
subtopics.teaching: Matching puzzles pair items from different categories using positive and negative clues.
subtopics.worked_example: If Ravi studies Maths and Priya does not study Science, the remaining subject assignments can be narrowed by elimination.
subtopics.pitfall: One matching clue should not be applied to unrelated categories.
subtopics.mastery: Create a grid or table and mark confirmed and impossible pairings.

subtopics.title: calendar and clock logic
subtopics.teaching: Calendar and clock puzzles use dates, weekdays, elapsed time, angles or cyclic patterns to derive answers.
subtopics.worked_example: If a meeting starts at 2:35 and lasts 50 minutes, it ends at 3:25; clock-angle questions require converting time into hand positions.
subtopics.pitfall: A 24-hour day and a 12-hour clock cycle use different representations of the same time.
subtopics.mastery: Track units and cycles carefully and distinguish elapsed time from displayed clock time.

subtopics.title: multi-condition puzzles
subtopics.teaching: Multi-condition puzzles combine several constraints, so a valid solution must satisfy all of them simultaneously.
subtopics.worked_example: If A must be before B, C cannot sit beside D, and E must occupy the third position, start with the fixed position and eliminate arrangements violating either relation.
subtopics.pitfall: Solving conditions one at a time without checking their interaction can produce false candidates.
subtopics.mastery: List every condition and verify the final arrangement against each one.

subtopics.title: figure patterns
subtopics.teaching: Figure-pattern questions identify visual changes in shape, position, count, orientation, shading or size.
subtopics.worked_example: If a shaded triangle rotates 90 degrees clockwise at each step while the number of dots stays constant, both features form the pattern.
subtopics.pitfall: A pattern may contain more than one simultaneous change.
subtopics.mastery: Track each visual attribute separately before predicting the next figure.

subtopics.title: mirror images
subtopics.teaching: A mirror image reverses left and right across the mirror line while preserving top and bottom orientation.
subtopics.worked_example: A word's mirror image has its left-right order reversed relative to the vertical mirror.
subtopics.pitfall: A vertical mirror does not swap top and bottom.
subtopics.mastery: Apply the correct axis of reflection before selecting an image.

subtopics.title: water images
subtopics.teaching: A water image reflects a figure across a horizontal line, reversing top and bottom while preserving left and right.
subtopics.worked_example: A capital letter's water image changes its vertical orientation but does not exchange its left and right sides.
subtopics.pitfall: Confusing water reflection with a mirror reflection gives the wrong orientation.
subtopics.mastery: Identify the reflection axis and track which dimensions reverse.

subtopics.title: embedded figures
subtopics.teaching: Embedded-figure questions ask whether a target shape appears within a more complex figure, possibly rotated or hidden among overlapping lines.
subtopics.worked_example: A small triangle may be present as part of several intersecting segments even when no separate triangle is drawn.
subtopics.pitfall: Extra lines do not invalidate a target shape if the required structure remains present.
subtopics.mastery: Trace the target's defining edges systematically rather than judging by overall appearance.

subtopics.title: paper folding
subtopics.teaching: Paper-folding problems predict the positions of holes or cuts after a folded sheet is unfolded by reversing each fold.
subtopics.worked_example: A hole punched through two folded layers may appear as corresponding holes symmetrically placed when the paper is fully opened.
subtopics.pitfall: Unfolding reverses the folds in reverse order.
subtopics.mastery: Track fold axes and reflect each mark across every fold line.
